benefit: Enabling places to connect with nature
summary: Spaces where adults and children can explore, play and learn, building emotional connection and future stewardship
Features that help people slow down, such as seating, pavilions, water features, picnic areas and varied paths
Woodland walks, natural sounds and forest therapy reduce stress and support mental and physical health; links to green social prescribing
Woodlands as settings for contemplation, wonder and a sense of connection to something larger than oneself
Hiking, birdwatching, cycling, running, camping, dog walking and nature apps offer relief from urban pressures
Trees provide cooling, shade and shelter from wind, helping people cope with rising temperatures
Trees absorb pollutants and improve airflow, acting as natural air purifiers in towns and cities
Paths, parking, ramps, benches, transport and clear signage that let people with disabilities enjoy woodlands
Native habitats, sensory experience and nature monitoring (for example trail cameras) build understanding of ecosystems
Leaf cover, tree type and soft woodland floors absorb sound and create quieter spaces, varying by season
People value woodland beauty in different ways, shaped by culture and memory; unmanaged areas may be read as neglect
Well-maintained, all-ability trails that stay usable after rain and support responsible use

benefit: Sense of place, belonging and ownership
summary: Time spent in and caring for a woodland builds attachment and encourages stewardship through planting and clean-ups

benefit: Social value in justice, equity and inclusion
summary: Shared spaces for marginalised and diverse groups; managing differing priorities through open communication; virtual tours for those who cannot visit
Woodlands protect heritage sites and act as living records of past ways of life, supporting identity and tourism
Signboards, outdoor classrooms and activities that teach all ages, especially children, about ecosystems
Foraging for berries, mushrooms and herbs supports wellbeing and local food economies, with care for sustainability
Woodland tourism and ecotourism create jobs and income while supporting conservation and family activities
Sustainable harvesting and coppicing provide local wood fuel and can help ease fuel poverty in rural areas
